subject: Critical Thinking
title: Cherry-Picking: The Art of Selective Evidence
description: A quick, practical guide to Cherry-Picking: The Art of Selective Evidence.

hook.text: 'Since 1998, global warming has slowed.' True — if you start from 1998, an unusually hot El Niño year. Otherwise, false.

buildup.text: Cherry-picking: selecting data that supports your claim while ignoring data that contradicts it.

discovery.text: It's different from lying — the individual facts may be true. The deception is in what's excluded.

twist.text: Pharmaceutical companies cherry-pick trials. Publish the positive ones, bury the negative ones. Legally.

climax.text: The fix: always ask 'What data is missing?' and 'Who chose this starting point and why?'

punchline.text: Half the truth is a whole lie.

quiz.question: What makes cherry-picking deceptive?
options: It selects only supporting evidence while hiding contradicting data

details.summary: Cherry-picking selects only evidence that supports a claim while ignoring contradictory data. It creates a convincing but fundamentally dishonest picture by exploiting the fact that evidence exists for almost any position.
details.whyItMatters: Cherry-picked evidence appears in scientific debates, political arguments, and advertising. Recognizing it prevents you from being misled by incomplete data.
takeaways: Any position can be supported by selectively choosing evidence
The absence of contradictory evidence is the giveaway
Systematic reviews are designed to prevent cherry-picking

faq.question: How can you tell if someone is cherry-picking evidence?
faq.answer: Look for missing context: are they citing one study while ignoring a dozen that contradict it? Do they present only the favorable time period from a longer dataset? Asking for the full picture reveals cherry-picking.

faq.question: How is cherry-picking different from confirmation bias?
faq.answer: Confirmation bias operates unconsciously, filtering evidence without your awareness. Cherry-picking can be deliberate, knowingly selecting favorable data while hiding the rest. Both distort conclusions but differ in intent.
